accepted.s: The doctrine of parens patriae is primarily associated with which of the following?
o: The State acting as guardian of persons unable to protect themselves
The Union’s power over residuary subjects
The reconciliation of conflicting constitutional provisions
The invalidation of laws enacted by a State legislature
accepted.x: Parens patriae means that the State acts as guardian of persons who cannot protect themselves. It is generally invoked in welfare and rights cases.
accepted.tq: Identify the doctrine from its precise meaning and field of application.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The doctrine of pith and substance is applied mainly to determine which of the following?
o: Whether a law has received the President’s assent
The true nature of a law in relation to Union-State legislative lists
Whether a constitutional amendment violates the basic structure
Whether a fundamental right has been waived
accepted.x: Pith and substance examines the true nature and character of a law to determine legislative competence under the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
accepted.tq: Match the doctrine with its principal constitutional field.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following best describes the doctrine of colourable legislation?
o: A law operating outside a State is always unconstitutional
A State law automatically prevails over a Parliamentary law
A law may be invalidated because its political motive is improper
A legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly
accepted.x: Colourable legislation embodies the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. It is concerned with legislative competence, not with the motive of the legislature.
accepted.tq: Distinguish legislative competence from legislative motive.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A State law having operation outside the State may nevertheless be valid when there is a sufficient connection between the State and the subject matter. This principle is known as:
accepted.x: The doctrine of territorial nexus permits a State law to operate beyond the State when a sufficient nexus exists between the State and the subject matter of the law.
accepted.tq: Apply the doctrine to an extra-territorial operation scenario.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The doctrine of harmonious construction requires courts to:
o: Prefer Fundamental Rights over every Directive Principle in all cases
Read apparently conflicting provisions so that both can operate
Treat all constitutional provisions as legally unenforceable
accepted.x: Harmonious construction seeks an interpretation under which apparently conflicting provisions, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, can operate together.
accepted.tq: Select the interpretation that preserves both apparently conflicting provisions.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which doctrine was identified in an APPSC question as reconciling Central and Provincial laws?
accepted.x: The doctrine of pith and substance is used to reconcile Central and Provincial, or Union and State, legislative powers by examining the true nature of the law.
accepted.tq: Recall the doctrine associated with Union-State legislative reconciliation.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

accepted.s: With reference to colourable legislation, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It primarily examines the personal motive of the legislators
It concerns the competence of the legislature to enact the law
It applies only to laws affecting Fundamental Rights
It permits indirect exercise of a prohibited legislative power
accepted.x: Colourable legislation concerns legislative competence. It does not principally examine motive, and it prohibits indirect exercise of a power that cannot be exercised directly.
accepted.tq: Use the competence-versus-motive distinction to eliminate the traps.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

accepted.s: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) is associated with which doctrine?
accepted.x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure even though it incidentally touched imports. The case illustrates pith and substance.
accepted.tq: Link the leading case to the doctrine rather than to the incidental subject involved.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

accepted.s: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Prohibition Act was upheld primarily because its true character related to:
accepted.x: The Prohibition Act was treated according to its true character as a public-health measure, although it incidentally touched the subject of imports.
accepted.tq: Separate the true nature of the law from its incidental effect.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

accepted.s: Which case is associated with the doctrine of territorial nexus in relation to tax on prize competitions conducted from outside the State?
o: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)
accepted.x: State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957) concerned taxation of prize competitions run from outside the State and is associated with territorial nexus.
accepted.tq: Distinguish similarly named cases by the doctrine and factual setting.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

accepted.s: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) is associated with harmonious construction in the context of reconciling:
accepted.x: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) reconciled temple-entry provisions under Article 25(2)(b) with the rights of religious denominations under Article 26(b).
accepted.tq: Start from the sure case-article pairing.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The true character of a law is determined by examining the whole Act, its object and its effect.
2. A.S. Krishna (1957) is associated with this approach.
3. The doctrine examines only the title given to the legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the true character is not determined merely by the title; the whole Act, its object and its effect are considered.
accepted.tq: Reject the narrow title-only formulation and retain the whole-Act test.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

accepted.s: The doctrine of eclipse provides that a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is:
o: Dormant and capable of revival when the constitutional bar is removed
Valid only after approval by the President
Automatically converted into a Directive Principle
accepted.x: Under the doctrine of eclipse, an inconsistent pre-Constitution law becomes dormant rather than completely extinct and may revive when the Fundamental Rights bar is removed.
accepted.tq: Distinguish dormancy from permanent invalidity.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly states the limitation clarified in Ambica Mills (1974) regarding the doctrine of eclipse?
o: It applies exclusively to constitutional amendments
It applies only to pre-Constitution laws
It applies only to post-Constitution laws
It applies only to State laws concerning taxation
accepted.x: Ambica Mills (1974) clarified that the doctrine of eclipse applies to pre-Constitution laws, not generally to post-Constitution laws enacted in violation of Fundamental Rights.
accepted.tq: Use the pre-Constitution versus post-Constitution distinction.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

accepted.s: The doctrine of severability means that when only a part of a law violates Fundamental Rights:
o: Only the offending part is declared void, if it can be separated
The entire law must always be struck down
The offending part is waived by the affected citizen
The law becomes dormant until Parliament re-enacts it
accepted.x: Severability permits the valid portion of a law to remain operative when the unconstitutional portion can be separated. R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957) is associated with this doctrine.
accepted.tq: Apply the separability test instead of assuming total invalidity.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

accepted.s: Which case is associated with the principle that Fundamental Rights cannot be waived?
accepted.x: In Basheshar Nath (1959), the principle was recognised that Fundamental Rights cannot be waived by an individual.
accepted.tq: Associate the non-waiver rule with its leading case.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT a federal interpretation doctrine?
accepted.x: Waiver is a doctrine concerning the interpretation of Fundamental Rights. Pith and substance, colourable legislation and territorial nexus are federal interpretation doctrines.
accepted.tq: Separate Fundamental Rights doctrines from Union-State competence doctrines.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

accepted.s:
Consider the following doctrines:
1. Pith and substance
2. Colourable legislation
3. Territorial nexus
4. Incidental and ancillary powers
Which of the above belong to the group of federal interpretation doctrines?
accepted.x: All four are federal interpretation doctrines. Repugnancy is also included among the doctrines used in resolving legislative relations between the Union and the States.
accepted.tq: Recognise the complete doctrinal group rather than selecting only the familiar pairs.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

accepted.s: The doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers implies that:
o: An incidental matter must always be placed in the Residuary List
Parliament has no power over matters not expressly listed
A legislative entry covers matters incidental to the subject expressly assigned to it
A State legislature can legislate on every subject connected with public order
accepted.x: A legislative power over a subject includes powers over matters incidental and ancillary to that subject. Legislative entries are given a wide meaning for this purpose.
accepted.tq: Apply the main-entry rule to an ancillary matter.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

accepted.s: Which cases are associated with the doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers?
o: R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and Calcutta Gas
accepted.x: R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and the Calcutta Gas case are associated with the principle that an entry includes matters incidental and ancillary to it.
accepted.tq: Identify the cases by the doctrine they illustrate, not by their subject alone.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

accepted.s: Under Article 254, in the event of repugnancy between a Parliamentary law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject, the general rule is that:
o: The Governor decides which law will operate
The State law prevails throughout India
The Parliamentary law prevails over the repugnant State law
accepted.x: Article 254 provides that, in case of repugnancy in the Concurrent List, the Parliamentary law prevails over the inconsistent State law.
accepted.tq: Ask which law prevails in a direct repugnancy conflict.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 254(2):
1. A State law on a Concurrent List matter may prevail in that State if it has received the President’s assent.
2. Parliament may subsequently override such a State law.
3. President’s assent makes the State law permanently immune from Parliamentary legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Parliament may later override a State law that has received the President’s assent.
accepted.tq: Watch for the absolute word “permanently” in the false statement.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the order of legislative fields from the Union to the State level, followed by the residuary position?
o: Union, State, Concurrent; residuary power with the Supreme Court
Concurrent, Union, State; residuary power with the President
Union, Concurrent, State; residuary power with Parliament
State, Concurrent, Union; residuary power with States
accepted.x: The order is Union List, Concurrent List and State List. Residuary legislative power belongs to Parliament under Article 248.
accepted.tq: Recall both the list hierarchy and the authority holding residuary power.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

accepted.s: Article 248 of the Constitution is associated with:
o: The binding force of Supreme Court decisions
The residuary legislative power of Parliament
The President’s assent to State laws
accepted.x: Article 248 vests residuary legislative power in Parliament.
accepted.tq: Match the Article number with its constitutional subject.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

accepted.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied in India in:
accepted.x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court in Golaknath (1967).
accepted.tq: Use the chronology of leading constitutional cases to identify the anchor case.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

accepted.s: Article 141 embodies the principle of stare decisis by providing that:
o: The law declared by every High Court binds all courts in India
Only advisory opinions of the Supreme Court are binding
Parliament must approve every Supreme Court judgment
The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India
accepted.x: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India, reflecting the principle of stare decisis.
accepted.tq: Link the doctrine to the exact constitutional effect of Article 141.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

accepted.s: The doctrine of pleasure in relation to civil services is primarily contained in:
o: Article 310, subject to safeguards under Article 311
accepted.x: Article 310 embodies the pleasure doctrine, while Article 311 provides safeguards for civil servants against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
accepted.tq: Pair the principal Article with its constitutional safeguard.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

accepted.s: Which statement correctly describes the doctrine of separation of powers as understood in Indian constitutional law?
o: It is completely rigid and excludes all overlap among organs
It is functional rather than rigid
It applies only to the executive and judiciary
It is not connected with the basic structure doctrine
accepted.x: Indian separation of powers is functional rather than rigid. Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) illustrates this approach, while separation of powers is also regarded as part of the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute “rigid” formulation and identify the Indian adaptation.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

accepted.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Ram Jawaya Kapur
B. State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C.
C. Golaknath
D. Kesavananda Bharati
accepted.x: Ram Jawaya Kapur was decided in 1955, State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. in 1957, Golaknath in 1967 and Kesavananda Bharati in 1973.
accepted.tq: Place the dated cases first and then verify the sequence.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

accepted.s: Which of the following doctrines is correctly matched with its foreign origin?
accepted.x: The doctrine of pith and substance was borrowed from Canada. Prospective overruling is associated with the United States, pleasure with England, and public trust with Roman law.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure foreign-origin pairing and eliminate the swapped origins.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

accepted.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Pith and substance — Canada
2. Prospective overruling — United States of America
3. Pleasure — England
4. Separation of powers — France
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
accepted.x: All four pairs are correct. Separation of powers is associated with Montesquieu of France, while the other three origins are Canada, the United States and England respectively.
accepted.tq: Check each origin individually, especially the thinker-country association.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

accepted.s: The doctrine of public trust is stated to have its origin in:
accepted.x: The doctrine of public trust has its origin in Roman law.
accepted.tq: Directly identify the origin of the less commonly tested doctrine.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

accepted.s: The basic structure doctrine is identified in the material with which foreign origin?
accepted.x: The basic structure doctrine is identified with Germany as its foreign origin in the given constitutional comparison.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the origin of basic structure from the origin of separation of powers.
accepted.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

accepted.s: Constitutional morality is best understood as:
o: Following the opinion of the numerical majority in every case
Giving priority to customary morality over constitutional text
Fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality
Applying only the personal morality of judges
accepted.x: Constitutional morality requires fidelity to constitutional values, even where those values conflict with prevailing or popular morality. The phrase is associated with Ambedkar, drawing on Grote.
accepted.tq: Distinguish constitutional values from popular or customary morality.
accepted.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

accepted.s: The phrase “constitutional morality” is associated with B.R. Ambedkar’s reference to:
accepted.x: Ambedkar used the phrase constitutional morality after Grote.
accepted.tq: Recall the thinker linked to the phrase through Ambedkar.
accepted.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

accepted.s: Which of the following cases is associated with the application of constitutional morality?
accepted.x: Constitutional morality was applied in Navtej Johar (2018), Sabarimala (2018) and NCT Delhi (2018).
accepted.tq: Identify the case from the interpretive tool it applied.
accepted.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

accepted.s: Transformative constitutionalism views the Constitution primarily as:
o: A document concerned only with administrative procedure
A tool for changing an unequal society
A mechanism for preserving all pre-Constitution social practices
A code that excludes judicial interpretation
accepted.x: Transformative constitutionalism treats the Constitution as an instrument for transforming an unequal society and advancing substantive constitutional values.
accepted.tq: Identify the purpose-based meaning of the doctrine.
accepted.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

accepted.s:
Which of the following cases are associated with transformative constitutionalism?
1. Navtej Johar
2. Joseph Shine
3. Sabarimala
accepted.x: Transformative constitutionalism was applied in Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Sabarimala.
accepted.tq: Treat the named-case list as a complete set and test every item.
accepted.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

accepted.s: After Minerva Mills, the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles was understood as:
o: Directive Principles being enforceable in preference to Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights being wholly superior and Directive Principles being irrelevant
Both being read harmoniously, with Fundamental Rights as means and Directive Principles as ends
Both being excluded from constitutional interpretation
accepted.x: After Minerva Mills, Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are read harmoniously. Fundamental Rights are described as the means and Directive Principles as the ends.
accepted.tq: Use the means-versus-ends comparison to identify the integrated interpretation.
accepted.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

accepted.s: Which one of the following is a criticism of constitutional morality?
o: It is considered subjective and a possible route to judicial overreach
It makes all Directive Principles directly enforceable
It gives unlimited legislative power to State governments
It prevents courts from referring to constitutional values
accepted.x: Critics argue that constitutional morality may be subjective and may provide a route to judicial overreach.
accepted.tq: Identify the recognised criticism rather than a consequence not stated.
accepted.sec: ■ Universal angles

accepted.s: The broader significance of constitutional interpretation doctrines is that they:
o: Replace the Constitution with conventions of foreign countries
Make every legislative dispute a matter of executive privilege
Keep federal lawmaking workable and determine how Fundamental Rights operate against laws
Remove the distinction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
accepted.x: These doctrines make federal lawmaking workable and establish the manner in which Fundamental Rights operate in relation to legislation.
accepted.tq: Select the option covering both stated dimensions of significance.
accepted.sec: ■ Universal angles

accepted.s: Which statement correctly describes the current position regarding a 2025–26 ruling applying these doctrines by name?
o: There is a current 2025–26 ruling applying all these doctrines by name
There is no current 2025–26 ruling applying these doctrines by name
Only the doctrine of territorial nexus has been applied in a 2025–26 ruling
Only the doctrine of waiver has been applied in a 2025–26 ruling
accepted.x: The current relevance assessment states that there is no 2025–26 ruling applying these doctrines by name.
accepted.tq: Test the precise current-affairs status without extending it beyond the stated position.
accepted.sec: ■ Universal angles
